periods.activity_title: Before We Read: Sports, Feelings and First Impressions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.103): pre-reading discussion — sports for fun versus competition.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick paired exchange: ask students which games they play and how winning or losing makes them feel. Take a few responses whole-class to surface the range of attitudes.
Read aloud the opening pages of “Change of Heart” (p.103–105), with students following in their textbooks. Pause briefly after introducing Prabhat to let the character settle.

Work through the “Let us read” pre-reading vocabulary task on p.103: pairs tick the correct meanings of ‘friendly matches’, ‘opponent’, ‘tally of marks’, and ‘sporting spirit’, then share and justify their choices whole-class.
Brief whole-class consolidation: connect the four vocabulary items to what the class has just read about Prabhat, noting which terms already describe or contrast with his attitude.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading oral questions in “Let us read” (p.103) are designed to surface personal experience before the story introduces Prabhat’s extreme win-at-all-costs attitude — let students speak freely before any judgment is offered. Watch for the vocabulary item ‘sporting spirit’: students commonly conflate it with rule-following rather than the fair and respectful engagement the story will develop. The deeper comprehension questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.108) are not covered in this sitting and make a strong self-study or independent reading task.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Story: Surya Arrives and Prabhat Cheats

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.105): four comprehension questions after Part I of the story.
Let us discuss (p.107): two questions on Surya’s attitude after Part II.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud Part II of the story (p.105–107), with students following, pausing at the moment Prabhat secretly changes the scoreboard to let the significance land.

Students answer the “Let us discuss” questions from p.105 in pairs: the true–false item on Prabhat’s tolerance for losing, what was special about the last Friday of each month, who kept the score, and whether Prabhat would want a rematch. Share answers whole-class.

Move to the p.107 “Let us discuss” questions on Surya: how Surya felt about playing and what Prabhat observed in him. Elicit responses and draw out the contrast between Surya’s joyful ease and Prabhat’s anxious seriousness.

periods.teacher_notes: The story makes Prabhat’s cheating visible but withholds moral judgment — the guilt comes from inside Prabhat himself, not from anyone catching him. Guide students to notice this narrative choice when discussing why Prabhat cannot sleep. The question ‘Do you think Prabhat wished to play another match?’ invites inference; accept multiple justified readings rather than a single correct answer.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Prabhat’s Change and Listening to a Sports Announcement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.108): extract-analysis questions on Prabhat’s character.
Let us listen (p.110): first listening — circle the chess pair chosen.

homework.task_brief: Let us listen (p.110): fill in the six-detail notes table from the announcement.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the two extract passages from “Let us think and reflect” (p.108) so students have the text fresh before analysis.

Work through the p.108 extract-analysis questions as guided whole-class discussion: Prabhat’s conditional approach to games, how he was feeling that night, and why Surya’s contentment in defeat surprised him so profoundly.

Transition to listening. Read the sports announcement (p.128 transcript) aloud twice at natural pace while students listen with textbooks closed. Students circle the chess pair from the three options given on p.110.
Take the chess-pair answer whole-class, then brief students on the note-taking table on p.110 — they will complete it for homework, re-reading the announcement transcript independently.

periods.teacher_notes: The extract on p.108 about Prabhat’s conditional game-playing (‘he would play only when sure of winning’) is the story’s clearest psychological diagnosis — students tend to spot the behaviour but miss its root in fear of failure rather than laziness. For the listening task, reading the transcript aloud yourself at a steady pace replicates the listening condition the textbook intends; ask students to resist writing during the first read and simply listen.

periods.activity_title: Using Polite Language and Writing Prabhat’s Diary Entry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.111): paired role-play using ‘please’, ‘thank you’ and ‘sorry’.
Let us write (p.112): complete Prabhat’s diary entry using the given phrases.

time_bands.activity: Briefly introduce the three ‘magic words’ context from p.111: display the prompts table on the board and model one exchange (request and response) so students understand the paired format.
Pairs take turns role-playing three situations each from p.111 — requesting, apologising, and thanking — using the sentence-frame prompts. Circulate and coach appropriate register and tone.
Read the incomplete diary entry on p.112 aloud together, and examine the eight phrases in the box. Discuss as a class which phrase-type goes in each gap before students write independently.

Students complete the diary entry individually. Two or three volunteers read their completed entries aloud; the class checks the logic and emotional arc — does the completed diary capture Prabhat’s guilt and confusion?

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task draws on the social situations in the story’s world — Vani, Hitesh, Nupur and others from the class appear in the prompts — which keeps the exercise anchored in the chapter context rather than feeling detached. For the diary task, students sometimes simply insert the phrases in order without checking sense; the pre-writing whole-class discussion of which phrase belongs where is essential scaffolding before independent writing begins.
materials: Blackboard or display surface for the prompts table

periods.activity_title: Word-Building and the Past Perfect Tense

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.109): circle the verbs in three sentences from the story.
Let us learn (p.109): arrange circled verbs into first-action / second-action columns.
Let us learn (p.109): fill in blanks using past perfect form of bracketed verbs.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.109): word-building puzzle — consecutive letters from BADMINTON, PHENOMENON, BASKETBALL.

time_bands.activity: Write the three story sentences on the board (p.109) and ask students to circle the verbs. Take answers, then introduce the concept: when two past actions occur, English marks which came first with the past perfect.

Students arrange the circled verbs from the three sentences into Column A (first/old action — past perfect) and Column B (second/new action — simple past), using the model row already given in the textbook as a guide.

Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences on p.109, applying the past perfect form of the verb given in brackets. Check answers as a class, focusing on the ‘had + past participle’ construction and the irregular forms.
Introduce the word-building puzzle task (p.109) briefly: show one example from BADMINTON on the board. Students will complete all three words for homework.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often confuse simple past and past perfect when both actions feel equally ‘old’ — the column-arrangement task forces them to sequence the actions explicitly before writing a form, which is more effective than explanation alone. The sentences on p.109 all come directly from the story’s events involving Prabhat and Surya, so connecting the grammar to what happened in the narrative keeps the exercise meaningful rather than abstract.

periods.activity_title: Sporting Heroes: Reading Bio-sketches and Discussing Resilience

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.113–114): read bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra; discuss qualities behind their success.

time_bands.activity: Students read the bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra on p.113–114 independently and silently. Ask them to underline one detail per bio-sketch that strikes them as surprising or admirable.

Whole-class discussion: what qualities helped each athlete succeed despite humble beginnings? Draw responses on the board as a shared list. Guide students to connect these qualities — perseverance, love of the game, resilience — to the sporting spirit Prabhat discovers through Surya.

Students write five to seven sentences in their notebooks: what ‘sporting spirit’ means to them personally, drawing on both the bio-sketches and the story. Two or three volunteers share; the class responds to whether the definition has shifted since the start of the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra both foreground early hardship before achievement — this is a deliberate pedagogical pairing with Prabhat’s story, which shows that joy in playing matters independently of trophies. Students who have not yet connected the broader theme of ‘sporting spirit’ to their own lives often find the real athletes more concrete and relatable entry points than the fictional character. The Arjuna Awardees link on p.114 is suitable for independent research at home or in the school library.

periods.activity_title: The Story’s Heart: Prabhat’s Transformation and Sporting Spirit

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect II (p.108): questions on Prabhat’s transformation, Surya’s attitude, and the story’s title.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the closing section of the story (p.107–108) — Prabhat joining hide-and-seek, joking at badminton, and earning the compliment of great sporting spirit — to bring the narrative arc into view.

Students discuss three of the “Let us think and reflect II” questions (p.108) in small groups: how Prabhat’s attitude affected his enjoyment of games, how Surya’s attitude differed from his, and why sporting spirit matters. Groups share a summary of their discussion.

Whole-class discussion on the final question: why is the title ‘Change of Heart’ suitable? Students offer interpretations and the class evaluates them against the story’s events, arriving collaboratively at what the change is and who experiences it most deeply.

periods.teacher_notes: The title question (‘Change of Heart’) is the richest interpretive question in the chapter and rewards open discussion — students often notice that only Prabhat changes, while Surya remains constant throughout, which sharpens the irony. The question ‘Do you think Prabhat’s approach to games was healthy?’ occasionally draws responses that defend winning at all costs; treat this as a genuine debate point rather than a wrong answer, and let the story’s own evidence do the persuading. The remaining “Let us think and reflect II” questions on cheating and the function of sporting spirit make excellent self-study or journal-writing tasks for students who want to go further.

items.source_lo: Student identifies character traits, infers motivation, and analyses narrative change using prose fiction as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prabhat’s fear of losing, his cheating, Surya’s joyful sportsmanship, transformation through observation.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Prabhat and Surya in ‘Change of Heart’. Write True or False for each statement.
1. Prabhat chose to participate only in games he was confident of winning.
2. Surya grew upset and stopped playing basketball when he performed poorly at it.
3. Prabhat secretly changed the scoreboard while Surya was distracted by a joke.
4. By the end of the story, Prabhat’s classmates said he had great sporting spirit.

options.text: By the end of the story, Prabhat’s classmates said he had great sporting spirit.
Prabhat chose to participate only in games he was confident of winning.
Prabhat secretly changed the scoreboard while Surya was distracted by a joke.
Surya grew upset and stopped playing basketball when he performed poorly at it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Prabhat played only games he was sure to win, even if they lasted a minute.
2. False — Surya was frankly hopeless at basketball yet his delight in the game never dimmed.
3. True — Prabhat changed the tally while everyone laughed at Surya’s joke.
4. True — After his transformation, Prabhat’s classmates gave him the very compliment of great sporting spirit.

items.source_lo: Student identifies character traits, infers motivation, and analyses narrative change using prose fiction as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prabhat’s fear of losing, his cheating, Surya’s joyful sportsmanship, transformation through observation.
items.item_stem: In ‘Change of Heart’, Prabhat wins the badminton match against Surya but cannot sleep that night. Surya, who lost, is cheerful and suggests they play again. What does this contrast reveal about the difference between Prabhat’s and Surya’s understanding of what makes a game worthwhile? Use details from the story to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Prabhat equates a game’s worth entirely with winning, so despite claiming victory he feels hollow and guilty because his win was dishonest. Surya, by contrast, finds his satisfaction in the act of playing itself — in the laughter, the effort, and the company — so losing leaves him content and eager to play again. The contrast shows that Prabhat’s win-centred view denies him genuine enjoyment, while Surya’s participation-centred view gives him pleasure regardless of the score.

items.item_stem: Work with a partner. You accidentally bumped into a classmate during the games period and caused them to drop their water bottle. Apologise sincerely, offer to help, and then thank them when they accept your apology. Your partner plays the classmate. Speak for about one minute each.

expected_elements: Uses ‘sorry’ with a brief explanation of what happened.
Offers a practical gesture of help (picking up the bottle).
Thanks the classmate when the apology is accepted.
Maintains a polite, calm tone throughout the exchange.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Prabhat, the day after the badminton match. You want to apologise to Surya for having cheated on the scoreboard, and you also want to thank him for showing you that playing joyfully matters more than winning. Role-play this conversation with a partner who plays Surya. Make sure your apology and thanks sound genuine, not mechanical. Speak for about two minutes.

expected_elements: Acknowledges the specific act of cheating on the scoreboard.
Expresses regret for the unfairness to Surya using appropriate register.
Thanks Surya by naming what he learned from watching him play.
Surya’s response (partner) accepts graciously and encourages a rematch.

items.item_stem:
Imagine you are Surya, writing in your diary the evening after the badminton match. You do not know the scoreboard was changed, but you noticed how tense Prabhat was throughout the game. Write a short diary entry of about five to seven sentences. Use the prompts below to organise your thoughts.
• How the match felt to you.
• What you noticed about Prabhat during the game.
• How you felt after the match ended, win or lose.
• What you hope might happen the next time you play together.

expected_elements: Uses first-person diary voice with date or address (‘Dear Diary’).
Reflects Surya’s joyful, relaxed attitude towards the game.
Mentions an observation about Prabhat’s seriousness or tension.
Ends with a forward-looking, friendly thought about playing again.

items.item_stem: Prabhat’s attitude towards games changes completely by the end of ‘Change of Heart’. Write a paragraph of about eight to ten sentences from Prabhat’s point of view, describing the moment he first joins a game of hide-and-seek with genuine enthusiasm. In your paragraph, show how his feelings during this game are different from how he used to feel before his change of heart. You may write freely in your own words.

expected_elements: Contrasts Prabhat’s old anxiety about losing with his new enjoyment.
Includes sensory or emotional details of playing hide-and-seek.
Shows that the score or outcome no longer dominates his thinking.
Writing is coherent, in first person, with a clear before-and-after sense.

items.item_stem:
The sentences below describe events from ‘Change of Heart’, but each one has a gap. Fill in each blank with the past perfect form of the verb given in brackets, so that the sentence correctly shows which action happened first.

1. Before Surya arrived at the school, Prabhat __________________ (never / lose) a single badminton match to anyone in his class.
2. By the time the games period ended, Prabhat __________________ (realise) that Surya genuinely enjoyed losing.
3. Prabhat felt guilty because he __________________ (change) the scoreboard without anyone noticing.
4. When his classmates complimented him on his sporting spirit, Prabhat __________________ (already / begin) to play games just for fun.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. had never lost. 2. had realised. 3. had changed. 4. had already begun.

items.item_stem: The bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra in ‘Let us explore’ (p.113–114) describe two athletes who succeeded despite very difficult beginnings. Choose ONE of the two athletes. Write an extended response of two to three paragraphs in which you: (a) describe one significant challenge the athlete faced early in life, (b) explain one quality that helped them overcome it, and (c) connect that quality to the idea of ‘sporting spirit’ that Prabhat learns in the story.

expected_elements: Names a specific early challenge from the chosen athlete’s bio-sketch.
Identifies a quality (e.g., perseverance, love of sport) with textual support.
Draws a clear link between that quality and Prabhat’s growth in the story.
Writing is organised in paragraphs with a coherent argument.

items.source_context: Bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra: humble beginnings, perseverance, sporting achievement.
items.item_stem: Design a one-page ‘Sporting Spirit Award’ profile for an Indian sportsperson you admire — this may be Deepika Kumari, Neeraj Chopra, or any other athlete you know. Your profile must include: (a) the athlete’s name and sport, (b) one challenge they faced and how they responded to it, (c) one quality from their life that connects to the idea of sporting spirit in ‘Change of Heart’, and (d) a one-sentence citation explaining why they deserve the award. You may add a sketch or diagram if you wish.

expected_elements: Profile includes name, sport, and one verified biographical detail.
Challenge and response are described with specific, accurate detail.
Link to sporting spirit is explicit and draws on the story’s theme.
Citation is one complete sentence in appropriate formal register.
